FLAREX - Interactive NASA Combustion Research Explorer

FLAREX is an interactive research platform developed by Team Solo Explorer for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It brings NASA's published microgravity combustion research into one accessible environment, helping users explore experiments, compare findings, understand fire-safety implications, and investigate their relevance to future space missions.

The platform organizes research from investigations such as BASS, BASS-II, FLEX, ACME, SAFFIRE, and SAME. Through interactive dashboards, experiment comparisons, scientific visualizations, and evidence-linked insights, FLAREX helps users understand how flames behave in microgravity and what existing research reveals about fire prevention, detection, and suppression.

An additional Flammability Explorer concept aims to let users investigate selected conditions—including oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, and material—and explore model-based predictions of flame-spread behaviour, supported by relevant NASA research evidence.

By connecting scattered research with interactive exploration and transparent, evidence-based analysis, FLAREX aims to make complex combustion science easier to understand and more useful for spacecraft fire-safety research and potential applications on the Moon, Mars, and Earth.
details:
FLAREX Interactive NASA Combustion Research Explorer

FLAREX is an interactive research platform developed by Team Solo Explorer for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Its goal is to make NASA's microgravity combustion research easier to explore, compare, understand, and apply to space fire-safety research.

What does it do and how does it work?

FLAREX brings published NASA combustion investigations into one organized environment. Users can explore experiments such as BASS, BASS-II, FLEX, ACME, SAFFIRE, and SAME; examine their objectives, experimental conditions, findings, and related research sources; and compare available measurements. Interactive dashboards and scientific visualizations help users understand how factors such as oxygen concentration, airflow, fuel properties, and microgravity conditions influence combustion.

The platform also organizes findings around three important fire-safety areas: prevention, detection, and suppression. Its mission-relevance section helps users investigate how available research relates to environments such as the International Space Station and future Moon and Mars habitats, while distinguishing documented evidence from potential applications.

An additional Flammability Explorer feature is being developed to let users investigate selected conditions, including oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow velocity, and material, through model-based flame-spread predictions. These predictions are intended to be clearly separated from NASA's experimentally reported measurements and supported by relevant research references.

Benefits and intended impact

FLAREX reduces the difficulty of navigating research scattered across multiple investigations and reports. It helps students, researchers, and space-safety enthusiasts identify relevant evidence, compare experimental results, recognize missing information, and better understand the challenges of fire safety beyond Earth. At scale, it could support research exploration and informed discussions about safer spacecraft and future lunar and Martian habitats. Its findings may also inspire further investigation into fire-safety applications on Earth.

Tools and technologies

The prototype uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS for the frontend, with Python and FastAPI for backend services. Research information is organized in structured JSON datasets and delivered through REST APIs. The development approach also uses interactive scientific visualizations and evidence-linked research records. Further model-based prediction capabilities are being developed as an extension of the research platform.

Creativity and design considerations

FLAREX combines a research explorer, comparison environment, mission-relevance analysis, and a developing predictive exploration feature rather than presenting NASA research as a collection of static documents. Our team considered scientific accuracy, source traceability, data availability, missing or incompatible measurements, usability, and the limitations of transferring microgravity findings to partial-gravity environments. We distinguish published experimental evidence, potential applications, and model-generated predictions so that users can explore the research without confusing estimates with verified results.
